title: AC, Transformers and the Power Grid

cards.h: How power travels hundreds of kilometres
cards.b:
A power station in Chhattisgarh lights a bulb in Chennai. The electricity must travel hundreds of kilometres without losing most of its energy on the way. The trick, invented in the 1880s, is to use alternating current and transformers.

Behind every wall socket is a continent-scale machine, the grid, tuned to run in perfect rhythm.

Direct current (DC) flows one way, as from a battery. Alternating current (AC) reverses direction many times a second, tracing a sine wave. In India the mains alternates at 50 Hz: 50 complete cycles every second. In the USA it is 60 Hz.

AC comes naturally from a generator, a coil turning in a magnetic field. Its great advantage is that a transformer can change AC voltage up or down cheaply. DC cannot do this easily.

AC voltage keeps changing, so what does '230 V' mean? It is the root mean square (rms) value, the steady DC voltage that would heat a resistor equally.

Peak and rms

V(rms) = V(peak) / square root of 2 = 0.707 x V(peak)

So 230 V rms mains actually swings up to about 325 V at its peak, then down to -325 V and back, 50 times a second. Appliances are rated by rms values.

A transformer has two coils wound on an iron core. AC in the first (primary) coil makes a changing magnetic flux in the core, which induces an AC voltage in the second (secondary) coil. This is Faraday's law at work.

Transformer rule

V2 / V1 = N2 / N1 (ratio of turns)
power in is about power out

More turns on the secondary gives a higher voltage and lower current (step-up); fewer turns gives the opposite (step-down). A good transformer is over 98 percent efficient. It works only with AC, since DC gives no changing flux.

cards.h: Why the grid uses high voltage
cards.b:
Power in a wire is P = V I, and heat lost in the wire is I squared times R. For the same power, raising the voltage ten times cuts the current ten times and the heat loss a hundred times.

So power stations step voltage up to hundreds of thousands of volts for long-distance lines, and substations step it down before it reaches your street, then again to 230 V.

cards.h: The war of the currents and the grid
cards.b:
In the 1880s Thomas Edison backed DC; George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla backed AC. The 'war of the currents' was won by AC because of transformers: only AC could be sent efficiently over long distances.

A modern grid links many generators, all spinning in step at exactly 50 Hz in India. If demand rises, the frequency dips; operators must instantly add supply. Keeping this balance is one of the great engineering feats of the age.

Send 100 kW through a line of 1 ohm total resistance.

At 230 V: current = 100,000 / 230 = 435 A. Loss = I squared R = 435 squared x 1 = about 189,000 W, more than the power sent. Impossible.

At 23,000 V: current = 4.35 A. Loss = 4.35 squared x 1 = 19 W. A loss ten thousand times smaller.

Step-down by a transformer with 10,000 turns on the primary to 100 turns: voltage ratio 100, so 23,000 V becomes 230 V.

• '230 V means the voltage is always 230.' It is an rms value; the instantaneous voltage swings to about 325 V.
  • 'Transformers make power.' They change voltage and current but not total power (apart from small losses).
  • 'A transformer works on a battery.' Only a changing current gives a changing flux; steady DC gives no output.

India completed its integrated national grid on 31 December 2013, when the Southern Grid was synchronised with the rest. Since then power can flow from surplus regions to deficit ones at one frequency, 50 Hz. India's main transmission lines include 400 kV, 765 kV and high-voltage DC links.

The Indian grid is now one of the largest synchronised grids in the world, and an increasingly important home to solar and wind power, which makes keeping the frequency steady harder.

• AC alternates; Indian mains is 230 V rms, 50 Hz; peak is about 325 V.
  • Transformers use Faraday's law: V2/V1 = N2/N1; they only work on AC.
  • High-voltage transmission slashes I squared R heat loss.
  • The grid is a synchronised machine, held at one frequency.
